rows: William Henry Fox Talbot laid plants on light-sensitive paper and let the sun print their shapes, long before cameras could make clear pictures. Every vein and edge of the plant shows up as a pale outline.
Pick one leaf or stem. Can you follow its edge all the way around?
Composition with a Hat

Hippolyte Bayard arranged hats, plaster casts and other objects on a table and photographed them in 1839, the year photography was announced. It is one of the first still lifes made with a camera, and he made it with his own method that printed pictures directly on paper.
Which objects can you name? Why do you think he picked them?

William Henry Fox Talbot photographed fruit sellers in England using the calotype, a paper negative he invented. The soft, grainy look comes from the paper itself, and the picture shows ordinary working people at a time when most photographs showed buildings.
What do you think the people are doing? Look at what is on the ground in front of them.
Talbot photographed this old library at Oxford University in 1838, early in his experiments. Buildings made good subjects because they could stand still for the many minutes a camera needed.
Why were buildings easier to photograph than people in the 1830s?

William Henry Fox Talbot made this picture of a chapel at Windsor Castle on paper he had coated with silver. He was one of the inventors of photography, and his paper negatives meant you could print many copies of one picture.
Count the pointed arches and windows. How many can you find?
Daguerreotype Locket

This tiny picture was made in the 1830s as a daguerreotype, a one-of-a-kind photograph on a polished silver plate, and then set into a locket. People wore them like a pocket-sized portrait gallery of someone they loved.
Why might someone want a picture small enough to wear?
Hippolyte Bayard photographed plaster casts of sculptures in 1839, the year photography was announced to the world. Statues were perfect early subjects because they never blinked or fidgeted.
What would be hard about photographing a living person in 1839?
David Octavius Hill and Robert Adamson photographed these sisters in Scotland in the early 1840s. They used paper negatives and soft light, and their portraits look as warm as paintings.
Look at their clothes. What kind of fabric do you think each dress is made of?
This daguerreotype from France shows a priest in dark robes. The picture is a mirror-like silver plate, so you have to tilt it to see the image. The sitter had to hold still for several seconds.
Try to sit perfectly still for ten seconds. How hard was it?
Bayard, Eyes Closed

Hippolyte Bayard made portraits of himself in the early 1840s. In his most famous picture he pretended to be a drowned man, because he felt the French government had ignored his invention. Here he poses with his eyes closed, as if asleep.
Why do you think he chose to close his eyes?
Bayard and His Statuettes
Hippolyte Bayard photographed himself among small plaster statues in 1842. He loved arranging pictures like little stage sets, and he taught himself how to make direct positive prints on paper.
Find the person in the picture. How is he standing next to the statues?
Hippolyte Bayard photographed a Paris square in 1842. Early exposures were so long that moving people vanish, so the streets look strangely empty even though Paris was busy.
Where are all the people? Why would a busy square look empty?
Junk Dealers on Rue du Rocher
Bayard photographed second-hand dealers and their goods on a Paris street. Pictures of ordinary street life were rare in the 1840s, so this one shows how the city really looked.
What do you think the dealers are selling?
Bouquet of Flowers
Bayard photographed a bunch of flowers in the early 1840s. Flowers hold still, so they were good practice for photographers whose cameras could not freeze motion.
Which flowers can you spot? How many different shapes are there?
This portrait by Hill and Adamson shows men from the Church of Scotland who left to form a new church in 1843. The two photographers made hundreds of portraits for a giant painting of the event.
Look at their faces. What mood do you see?

James Nasmyth was an engineer who invented the steam hammer, and he sat for these pioneering photographers in the 1840s. Hill and Adamson posed people in soft shadow, like a painting, to make portraits that felt alive.
What do you think an inventor might hold or wear? Look for clues.

Hill and Adamson photographed Elizabeth Rigby, a writer and art critic, in Scotland. She later became one of the first women to write about photography as an art. Their portraits made photography look like fine art.
How is she posed? Does she look serious or friendly?

William Henry Fox Talbot photographed glass bottles and glasses on a shelf. He published this picture in the first book illustrated with photographs, called The Pencil of Nature, to show what a camera could do.
What makes glass tricky to photograph? Look at the reflections.
Mathew Brady photographed Caleb Lyon, a congressman, in his New York studio. Brady made daguerreotypes of many famous Americans in the 1840s and hung them in his gallery.
What do you think a politician wanted to look like in a portrait?
The Open Door
Talbot photographed a wooden door held open by a broom at his home, Lacock Abbey. He wrote that the camera could capture things artists might want to paint, and this picture is one of his best known.
What do you notice leaning near the door?
Mathew Brady photographed Clement Clay, a senator from Alabama. Brady believed photography could record the faces of a whole nation, and he made hundreds of portraits of politicians.
Is the senator smiling? Why might serious faces have been common?
This portrait shows a U.S. Army colonel who became famous in the Mexican-American War. Early photographs let people see the faces of leaders they had only read about.
What clues tell you he was a soldier?
Lacock Abbey
William Henry Fox Talbot photographed the old abbey where he lived. This is one of the first photographs of a building made by the inventor himself, and it shows what he saw out of his own window.
Talbot lived here. What would you like about having an old abbey as a home?
Cassius Marcellus Clay was an American abolitionist who spoke out against slavery. Mathew Brady's studio photographed leaders like him so that the public could see their faces.
Why would people want a picture of someone they only knew from the news?
Horace Greeley
Horace Greeley was a famous newspaper editor, and Brady photographed him sitting in a chair with a tall hat. Brady's portraits helped make faces from the news feel real.
What do you think he is looking at?
Southworth and Hawes were two of the best daguerreotype makers in Boston. They made large, sharp, beautifully lit portraits, and their pictures are among the best in the world from the 1840s.
Is this plate sharper than you expected for 1845?
This daguerreotype shows an apothecary, or old-fashioned pharmacy, with its owner. Photographers like this one traveled to shops and homes, so we can see what everyday places looked like.
What might a pharmacy have sold in 1845?
Newhaven Fishwives

Hill and Adamson photographed fishermen's wives in the Scottish village of Newhaven in 1845. The women sold the catch and carried heavy baskets. These pictures are among the first to show the daily lives of working people.
What do you think is in their baskets? Look at how they stand.
This French hunting party posed with a badger in the Loire Valley. Hunting scenes were popular with painters, and this early photograph acts like a small stage with people and dogs.
Who is holding what? Look for the dogs.
The Beach at Newhaven
Hill and Adamson photographed fisher families on the beach at Newhaven, with boats and nets in the background. Their paper negatives gave the pictures soft light, like early paintings.
What are the people doing on the beach?

Hill and Adamson photographed Scots Guards soldiers at Edinburgh Castle in 1846. A group portrait with a camera was much faster than painting each soldier, so photography began to replace painted portraits.
Why would a camera be quicker than a painter?
The two Scottish photographers visited this ruined castle in 1846. They liked old buildings because the soft paper negatives made them look moody and ancient.
What mood does the ruined castle give you?
Hippolyte Bayard photographed a fountain behind Notre-Dame in Paris in 1847. His views of the city are some of the oldest we have, showing it before big rebuilding changed the streets.
What would you see if you stood here today?
Alcázar of Seville
Talbot photographed this Spanish palace, with its decorated arches, in 1848. Pictures of far-off landmarks made travelers at home feel as if they had been there.
Look at the arches. What patterns can you spot?
Louis-Rémy Robert photographed this fountain in Brittany in the late 1840s. Photographers like him hoped their pictures could be turned into prints that anyone could buy.
Where does the water come from in this picture?
Henri Le Secq photographed a farm built into the soft rock of the French countryside. He had been a painter, and he used the same eye for shape and shadow.
Where does the building stop and the rock begin?
Portrait
Antoine Samuel Adam-Salomon trained as a sculptor before he took up photography. He lit faces like carved busts, with dramatic shadows that made his portraits famous.
Which side of the face is lit? Which is in shadow?
A French military officer posed for this early portrait. Soldiers liked to have a picture to send home, and the stiff pose is partly because they had to hold still.
What details of the uniform can you see?

This picture shows a gorge in the Pyrenees mountains, where British tourists came for their holidays. Early photographers carried heavy cameras to scenery like this, so that people at home could see it.
What would it be like to carry a camera up here?

Gustave de Beaucorps photographed a woman in Algeria in about 1850. Photographs from this time often show the clothing and customs of people across the world, though they were chosen by the photographer.
What details of clothing do you notice?
A man on a black horse poses in front of a doorway. Pictures of people on horseback had long been popular with painters, and early photographers copied the idea.
How does the horse stand? Is it calm or restless?
Mother and Child with Flowers
A child stands on a chair holding flowers, with a mother beside. Daguerreotypes became cheap enough that ordinary families could have a portrait for the first time.
What do you think the child is holding?
A mother poses with two children in a portrait by Jean-Baptiste Frénet. He was a painter who switched to photography, and his skill with composition shows.
How are the three of them arranged?
The Sodhis of Anandpur Sahib
Francis Frith photographed people and places in the Punjab in northern India. Frith was one of the first big travel photographers, and his prints sold across Britain.
What do the clothes tell you about these people?
Samadhi of Maharaja Ranjit Singh, Lahore
This shrine in Lahore marks the resting place of Maharaja Ranjit Singh, a ruler of the Sikh Empire. Early photographs of buildings like this give a picture of how they looked long ago.
What shapes do you see in the roof and walls?
Tomb of Shah Abdool Wahab
A domed tomb in the Punjab, photographed with a large camera and printed on albumen paper. Photographers carried glass plates on carts and camels to reach places like this.
How many domes or arches can you count?
Theseus from the Parthenon
This French photograph shows a statue from the Parthenon in Athens. It is one of the first pictures to record famous sculptures, so people could study them without traveling to see them.
Does the sculpture look alive? How can you tell?

Charles Marville photographed a stone doorway that was once part of a grand château and now stands in a Paris school. Marville is best known for recording old Paris streets before they were torn down.
How can a piece of one building end up in another?
Studying the Muscles of Expression

Guillaume Duchenne used small electric shocks to make faces smile or frown, then photographed them. He wanted to find out how our faces make feelings. His pictures of expressions were one of the first science projects done with a camera.
Make the same face. Which muscles move?
Studying the Muscles of Expression II
Duchenne photographed how single muscles move the face when stimulated. His book showed readers the difference between a real smile and a fake one, and Charles Darwin later used his pictures.
Do you know how to tell a real smile from a fake smile?
Benjamin Brecknell Turner took up photography as a hobby and carried a huge camera around the English countryside. His pictures show quiet scenes of trees, cottages and rivers.
What is the weather like in this picture?
The Louvre: Clock Pavilion
Édouard Baldus photographed the Louvre in Paris while it was being rebuilt. The French government hired him to record important buildings, and his sharp prints helped win photography respect.
What would you want to see inside this building?
Notre-Dame, Paris
Édouard Baldus photographed the side of Notre-Dame cathedral with its tall flying buttresses, the stone arms that hold the walls up. He printed the picture from a large glass negative.
Can you find the stone arms that prop up the walls?
A Temple in India
William Henry Pigou was a doctor and a part-time photographer working for the British in India. His pictures are some of the earliest of Indian temples.
What details do you notice on the temple walls?
Charles Delahaye
Charles Marville photographed a man named Charles Delahaye in 1852. Before he became known for street scenes, Marville made portraits, and this is one of them.
What does the sitter's expression tell you?
The Tomb of Itimad-ud-Daulah
John Murray was a doctor who photographed the Taj Mahal and other great buildings in India. This tomb in Agra is sometimes called the baby Taj, and Murray's large prints sold across Britain.
Look at the patterns on the walls. What shapes repeat?
Angel, Sainte-Chapelle
Auguste Mestral was one of five photographers hired by the French government in 1851 to record historic buildings. He photographed an angel sculpture in the Sainte-Chapelle in Paris.
How would you pose like this angel?
Kom Ombo
Francis Frith traveled up the Nile in the 1850s and photographed temples half buried in sand. Kom Ombo is a temple to the crocodile god, and people in Britain were thrilled to see it.
Why would people in Britain want to see this picture?
Mainz Market
Charles Marville photographed the old market square in Mainz, Germany. The weekly market had been held there for centuries, and his picture records houses that were later lost.
What buildings do you see around the square?
Amiens Cathedral, Central West Portal
The Bisson brothers, Louis-Auguste and Auguste-Rosalie, climbed with huge cameras to photograph French cathedrals. This doorway at Amiens is covered with saints and kings.
How many carved figures can you count?
Chartres Cathedral, South Transept
The Bisson brothers photographed the south side of Chartres Cathedral. Their large photographs let people study carved details without climbing a scaffold.
Can you find any carved saints in the doorway?
Chartres Cathedral, West Façade
This is the front of Chartres Cathedral in France, built more than 800 years ago. The Bisson brothers needed bright sunshine and a lot of patience to photograph it.
The two towers are different. Can you spot how?
Arch of Septimius Severus, Rome
The Bisson brothers photographed an ancient Roman arch built in the year 203. Their pictures showed travelers the ruins of Rome in sharp detail.
What did this arch celebrate? Look at the carved figures.
Water Mills in Auvergne
Édouard Baldus photographed old water mills in the Auvergne region of France. His pictures mix people's work with the land, and the water looks silky because of the long exposure.
Why does the water look smooth like silk?
Roger Fenton photographed British officers in the Crimean War in 1854 and 1855. He was one of the first war photographers and had to haul a wagon-sized darkroom.
Why would a photographer need a wagon for a camera?
General Charles Hind
Roger Fenton photographed generals and soldiers in Crimea in 1855. He did not show fighting because cameras were too slow, but his portraits put faces on a distant war.
What do you notice about the general's uniform?
Cavalry Camp, Balaklava
Roger Fenton photographed a cavalry camp during the Crimean War. The horses and tents tell us how soldiers lived, even though cameras of the time could not capture battles.
What would life in this camp be like?
Cavalry Camp, Toward Kadikoi
Fenton's camp pictures show lines of tents and horses on the hills of Crimea. The war lasted from 1853 to 1856, and his photographs were seen by people at home in Britain.
Can you find the horses?
General Sir Charles Ash Windham
Roger Fenton photographed this British general in the Crimea in 1855. Windham was known for leading an attack during the war.
What do you see in the general's face?
Church of the Madeleine
Baldus photographed the Madeleine in Paris, a church that looks like a Greek temple. He chose a calm view so that the columns lined up like a row of soldiers.
How many columns do you see?
Yenangyaung Monastery, Burma
Linnaeus Tripe produced some of the earliest photographs of British India and Burma. This monastery building, called a kyaung, was photographed on a trip to document the region.
What material do you think the building is made of?
Court of the Lions, Alhambra
Charles Clifford photographed the famous courtyard of the Alhambra in Granada, Spain. The slender columns and the fountain of lions made it one of Europe's most photographed places.
How many columns can you count?
